questions.q: What was the response of Nahash the Ammonite to the request for a covenant from the men of Jabesh?
questions.a: He said he would make a covenant with them if he could gouge out all their right eyes and bring disgrace on Israel.

questions.q: How did the elders of Jabesh respond to Nahash’s proposal?
questions.a: They asked for seven days to send messengers throughout Israel to see if anyone would save them.

questions.q: Why were the people in Saul’s town of Gibeah weeping?
questions.a: They were weeping because they had heard the words of the men from Jabesh.

questions.q: How did Saul respond to the threat against Jabesh?
questions.a: The Spirit of God rushed upon him, he became very angry, and he persuaded the men of Israel and Judah to fight.

questions.q: What message did the messengers bring back to the men of Jabesh?
questions.a: They told the men of Jabesh that they would have deliverance the next day by the time the sun was hot.

questions.q: What did the men of Jabesh say to Nahash the Ammonite?
questions.a: They told Nahash that they would come out to him the next day, and he could do to them whatever seemed good to him.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the battle between Israel and the Ammonites?
questions.a: The people of Israel attacked and defeated the Ammonites, and the survivors were totally scattered.

questions.q: Why did Saul say that none of the men who opposed him would be put to death?
questions.a: Saul said no one would be put to death, because that day Yahweh had brought deliverance to Israel.

questions.q: Why did Samuel, Saul, and all the people of Israel go to Gilgal?
questions.a: They went to Gilgal to renew the kingship, make Saul king before Yahweh, and sacrifice peace offerings.

commentary.text: Verses 1–11 The first fruit of Saul's government was the rescue of Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonites. To save their lives, men will part with liberty, and even consent to have their eyes put out; is it then no wisdom to part with that sin which is as dear to us as our right eye, rather than to be cast into hell-fire? See the faith and confidence of Saul, and, grounded thereon, his courage and resolution. See also his activity in this business. When the Spirit of the Lord comes upon men, it will make them expert, even without experience. When zeal for the glory of God, and love for the brethren, urge men to earnest efforts, and when God is pleased to help, great effects may speedily be produced.

They now honoured Saul whom they had despised; and if an enemy be made a friend, that is more to our advantage than to have him slain. The once despised Saviour will at length be acknowledged by all as the Lord's own anointed king. As yet, upon his mercy-seat, he receives the submission of rebels, and even pleads their cause; but shortly, from his righteous tribunal, he will condemn all who persist in opposing him.
